title: Finding the Swing coffee house in Tokyo and the Lewis band
summary: Green hears Lewis records in a Shibuya coffee house, then finds the band at its hotel and plays piano with George.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Okay, so then, now tell us about the—you went to Japan. You were into France. You were in Japan at the same time the store was there, weren't you?

I was in Japan visiting a cousin who lives in Tokyo in 63. This was the summer, I think August 63. And, uh, was wandering around Shibuya, which is the area in which he lived. And each—this is a small section of Tokyo, and it has its own small bar district and red light district, whatever. And it's up a hill behind some buildings and it's alleyways. And I was walking alone, feeling very western and very out of place. When suddenly this same sound that I'd heard in 1945 comes banging out onto the street. And it's a record of bunk and George Lewis. And it froze me in my tracks, was the last thing I expected to hear. And, again, blindly, I—there was a doorway and I just went in. And there was this smoke-filled room, oh, twenty feet by twenty, if that. Tables. Many Japanese sitting at it, drinking coffee. It was the swing coffee house in Shibuya. Later I found there were two coffee houses in the chain. This was one of them. And the little waitress came up to me. Her name, it turned out later, was Sayuri Yamamoto. And on the walls—I stood there and she asked me what I wanted and I couldn't talk. On the walls were pictures of George Lewis, bunk. In the back, over on the left, was a turntable, which—with, uh, against the wall a couple of huge speakers and a rack of records. And all of these records were George Lewis and Bunk Johnson. But there were more George Lewis records there than anything else. I couldn't believe it. And this is—this was their stock and trade. Japanese would come—come to the swing coffee house in Shibuya to listen to records and drink this tall iced coffee over—overly sweetened. They sat there. So, uh, they had some pictures of George on the wall and they had a excerpt centerfold from Time—Life magazine had done a story on New Orleans jazz and there it was not even framed. And, uh, you just pasted it on the wall. So, the little waitress, Sayuri Yamamoto, noticed how interested I was and, uh, said, George Lewis, I—I said, I—I—I know him. I've—I've heard him play. And, uh, she told me, and, uh, she told me, and very hesitant in English, he was coming to Japan, which was the first knowledge I had. I said, if he comes to Japan, if he comes to Tokyo, I'm sure I will see him. And our eyes lit up—someone who might know George Lewis. I said, somehow I will bring you his autograph and you can put it up on the wall next to the pictures. I left. Called the American Embassy. They didn't know when Lewis was coming to Japan. Finally, I forget how, I found the hotel that they were going to stay at. The name escapes me. And called the hotel and they had arrived the previous day or were to arrive the following day, whatever—this was several days after the initial encounter at the Swing. And I went over there and there was Jaffe and Sandy and George Lewis, uh, Manny Sales, Joe Watkins, Papa John Joseph, Joe Robichaux, Punch Miller, whoever left out, and, uh, Louis Nelson. And this was the band that was to tour Japan. It was—they had arrived—when I arrived at the hotel, they had arrived in Japan the previous day. And they had obviously been very tired. This was the following evening, late afternoon. And here they were in a foreign country, not knowing where to go, feeling a little bit lonely, a little bit out of place. Saw George, we greeted one another. I had played with George during that first visit to Preservation Hall. New Orleans was still segregated at that time. And somehow the band had stopped playing. George was putting away his clarinet. I got to the piano and I remember playing Whining Boy. And George put together his clarinet. And Jaffe's closed the shutters and we played together, which was a very moving experience, because it was really just the second time I'd seen him since the bunk days. That was the first time you've played with him. That was the first time I played with him. So that when I did greet him in the hotel in Japan, he knew who I was. I certainly knew who he was. And it was a nice hello. They were thinking, where should they go that evening? And I said, well, I don't know whether you'd be interested. I knew quite well they probably would be. I said, but there's a little coffee house, which I think I can find, which I think would entertain you. I have nothing but your records there, George, and your pictures on the wall. And they worship you there. So everyone's eyes lit up. Let's go. We piled into two taxi cabs. And about nine o'clock, I forget what day of the week this was, I don't think it was a weekend, probably a Thursday night, something like that. We arrived at the Swing coffee house.
